finalResponse:
# Notes Before the Model Is Finished

*Written now, on purpose. A transition plan written after the model is complete isn't a plan — it's a defence of the model, and by then somebody's spreadsheet has become somebody's position.*

---

## The number everyone will stare at is the least interesting one

There are three troughs in this transition and the room will conflate them for the next two years unless we separate them in week one.

**The recognised revenue trough** is an accounting event. Money we would once have booked on Tuesday is now booked over thirty-six months. Nothing has been destroyed. This is the deepest-looking trough, the one that ends up on the front of the analyst note, and the most nearly fictional.

**The cash trough** is real. If we go from cash-upfront to cash-monthly, we are handing our customers an interest-free loan on a scale we have never previously extended, and we have to fund it. This is the constraint. It is also, quietly, the most tractable — because a three-year prepaid subscription solves it entirely and costs us a discount.

**The demand trough** would be the only one that matters, and there's no reason to have one. If it appears, we did something wrong to our installed base, and no pricing cleverness will get it back.

Most transitions are governed as though the first trough were the third. The whole plan below is an attempt to make the first one shallow enough to survive, the second one funded, and the third one impossible.

The other thing worth saying before the modelling hardens: **the trough is not weather. It's a dial.** Its depth is a direct function of how fast we convert and how much upfront recognition we permit ourselves along the way. Anyone presenting it as a forecast rather than a choice has misunderstood the exercise, and I'd gently want to know why.

---

## An assumption I'd rather state than discover

That competitor lost a fifth of its installed base. I'd want to know how many of that fifth were paying us — sorry, them — anything at all in the preceding year.

My working assumption, until someone shows me otherwise, is that our own installed base is partly fiction. There is a licensed base and there is a *paying* base, and the gap between them is customers running a four-year-old version who dropped maintenance in a cost cycle and never came back. They are on the logo slide. They are not on the cash statement. When they leave, they leave a hole in a chart and nowhere else.

So the first piece of work isn't commercial, it's arithmetic: segment the base by *maintenance-paying status, version currency, and seat utilisation*. I'd expect three populations to fall out —

- **Current and engaged.** Paying maintenance, running recent versions, using their seats. These are the conversion target and essentially all of the value.
- **Paying but dormant.** Maintenance current, version stale, utilisation low. Highest churn risk *and* highest upside — they are one conversation from either outcome.
- **Lapsed.** Already gone, still counted.

If the third group is fifteen per cent of the base and two per cent of revenue, then the competitor's catastrophe was substantially a reclassification, and we should say so internally before the number is used to frighten the board into half-measures. Half-measures are how these transitions actually fail.

---

## Offer structure: three doors, and nobody is pushed through one

The grievance is the risk. Not the price. Nobody churns because a subscription costs more; they churn because they were told that the thing they bought — and defended internally, and built a process around — was retroactively a mistake.

**Door one: the perpetual licence keeps working. Forever. In writing.**

I'd publish something short and unhedged. Call it whatever the lawyers can tolerate. The content: *what you bought, you own. It runs offline, indefinitely, on the version you're entitled to, with no phone-home kill switch, no feature revocation, and no expiry.* That costs us nothing — the software is already written — and it removes the single narrative that spreads fastest in user forums and procurement teams.

The honest corollary, stated in the same breath: **the perpetual asset is frozen in amber.** It doesn't get new capability. Everything we build from the announcement date onward ships to subscription. That's not a punishment, it's simply what "perpetual" always meant, said out loud for the first time.

Maintenance for existing holders continues to be sold, and continues to escalate on its normal schedule. We do not need to force anyone. We need only stop subsidising staying.

**Door two: term licence — the bridge instrument nobody remembers to use.**

A one- or three-year on-premise licence, invoiced in advance, with support attached. For a distinct on-prem software licence, the licence component of a term arrangement can generally be recognised at a point in time with support taken ratably. That single structural fact is worth more to the shape of our P&L than any discount schedule in this document — and I'd want it validated with the auditors *before* it appears on a slide, not after. If it holds, term licences let us convert cash-and-behaviour years ahead of converting our revenue recognition, which is exactly the sequence we want.

It also gives the enterprise segment somewhere to go. Large customers with capex budgets, air-gapped environments and eighteen-month procurement cycles cannot move to cloud subscription on our timetable. Offering them only a door they can't walk through is how you manufacture the churn you were trying to avoid.

**Door three: full subscription.** Cloud-entitled, identity-based, continuously updated, the only door where the new things are.

Three doors, visibly open, with the economics arranged so that door three is obviously the sensible one. Choice preserved; outcome steered. This is the whole trick and it is not complicated.

---

## Migration incentives: a credit that decays, and a first year that's cheaper

Let perpetual list = 100, annual maintenance = 20.

**The loyalty credit.** A converting customer's perpetual licence becomes a permanent, per-seat discount against subscription — not a one-off rebate. It should feel like an asset that transferred, because rhetorically that's what we need it to be. And it should **decay on a published schedule**: full value if converted in the first four quarters, stepping down thereafter, gone by quarter twelve. Urgency generated by our own calendar rather than by a threat to their entitlement. Autodesk's trade-in ran roughly this shape and the decay did more work than the discount.

**The year-one rule.** For a converting maintenance-paying customer, *the first subscription year costs less than the maintenance year they just paid.* Say 18 against 20. Then escalators: 26, 32, 38, settling around 38–42.

This looks like we're giving money away. What we're actually doing is removing the only sentence a procurement officer needs to kill the conversion — "it went up" — and replacing it with a decision that's easy to approve and hard to unwind. The uplift arrives in years two and three, contractually pre-agreed, when the customer is inside the product, using the new capability, and the switching cost has quietly moved.

Steady-state target of ~38–42 against a 100/20 perpetual gives roughly a three-year payback versus the old model and materially better five-year value. That's the anchor. It's also the number the customer's own analyst will compute, so I'd rather we hand them the calculation than let them discover it feeling clever.

**Multi-year prepaid, discounted hard.** Three years paid upfront at, say, 12% off total. This is the cash lever and it is enormously underrated. It does nothing for recognised revenue — it fills the second trough while leaving the first one visible, which is precisely the trade we want, because the second one is the one that can actually stop us.

**And one thing I'd hold back.** Don't discount to the dormant segment first, however tempting the conversion count looks. Convert the engaged base first, at close to list, and let the resulting reference cases do the persuading. Cheap early conversions set a price expectation that propagates through the base within a quarter, and it never comes back up.

---

## Sales compensation: the motion splits before the plan does

The instinct will be to redesign the comp plan. I'd redesign the *organisation* first, because otherwise we're paying hunters to do administration and wondering why it's expensive.

**Split the two motions.** Converting a known, maintenance-paying customer is not selling. It's a scheduled, high-volume, low-touch account conversation with a deadline attached. It belongs to a dedicated install-base team, largely inside, compensated on volume and retention. New-logo acquisition stays with the field. Trying to run both through one comp plan produces a plan that motivates neither.

**Pay the field on cash, not on recognition.** Commission on total contract value of multi-year deals, paid on invoice. This aligns the rep with the exact behaviour that funds the transition, and it happens to preserve their take-home in the year they'd otherwise revolt. Two problems solved by one mechanic.

**Hold harmless, on a published taper.** Year one, on-target earnings protected at prior levels with conversion credit counted generously. Year two, 80%. Year three, the new plan stands alone. The taper must be published at the start. A hold-harmless that gets extended quietly teaches everyone to wait; a hold-harmless that ends unexpectedly loses the top quartile in a single quarter, and it's always the top quartile that has somewhere else to go.

**Clawback on twelve-month churn**, and a retention component in the plan from day one. Otherwise we will convert customers into churn with great efficiency and pay bonuses for it.

**Steering weights, adjusted quarterly and treated as a dial, not a policy.** Converted ACV at 1.0x, new-logo ACV at 1.5x, multi-year prepaid at a premium. If conversion is running slow we move the weight. This is where I'd want genuine latitude held by whoever runs the transition rather than routed through an annual comp committee — the whole point of a dial is that someone can turn it.

**The pre-announcement problem.** The moment the field infers a change, they will pull perpetual deals forward and hoard. That builds a spike and then a cliff, and the cliff will be read externally as demand collapse. Two defences: raise perpetual list *before* the announcement rather than discounting it away, and get the comp plan in front of the field before they work it out for themselves. They will work it out for themselves. They always do, and roughly a quarter earlier than anyone expects.

---
